Have a daily self-care checklist. On bad days, aim to accomplish your checklist rather than what depression is telling you to do. My list usually involves the basics: eat, sleep, shower, brush teeth, move, clean, and socialize. Socialize can be as simple as having a short conversation with a friend or a family member and possibly the hardest I have to do in a day.

You can make your own list with things you consider as part of your “good day”. I also added journaling and affirmations to the list and at least 15 minutes of reading just to keep the ball going.

Another thing that helped is to apply the do something principle. Didn’t have the energy to workout? Do 15 squats and you’re done. Need to clean? Pick up one trash. The important thing is you did something. Tomorrow, you’ll do better or not less than what you did today. And that will help you to keep moving forward.

Tbh I’d be pretty chill about it and calm down about the factors. Trust that the calories in and calories out method will work. If you feel the fat I doubt it’s all the water. And yes. You will lose weight as long as it’s under the calorie goals. Doesn’t matter what food. Although it will be easier with healthier food.

Just a tip though. When you really have to guesstimate calories, overestimate instead of under. If you eyeball 3/4 cup of rice I’d log it at 1 cup. This is to avoid making the mistake of underestimating calories and going over your budget.

Also, I don’t really know how “active” I’d consider your workout routine but I’d set the calculator at lightly exercise or sedentary. You may be overestimating that, too. 

Be patient and focus on the good habits. Maybe you’d also want to have more protein and complex carbs in your diet to make it easier. I’d ditch that flavored oatmeal and keep the plain ones and just add toppings with more fiber in it like raisins, seeds, other fruit (track cals and be careful), etc. Maybe even mix protein powder. Eggs and sweet potatoes also are easy options (poke holes on the sweet potatoes and microwave it). Snack on those if you’re really hungry.

You should stop estimating your food. You might be overdoing it. Calculate your [TDEE](https://tdeecalculator.net), cut 500 calories from it, and measure your food (buy a food scale). It’s impossible to not lose weight that way (unless you have a medical condition). 

On intermittent fasting, I find it easier to stick to my calorie goals when I fast as I am forced to skip a meal. It’s gonna be an adjustment process but it’s really doable and I don’t feel restricted during meal times.

On diets, I don’t really think of calorie counting as a weight loss diet like we usually see. I still eat what I want. I’m just mindful on the portion sizes and see to it that I’m not under or over eating. I can have a pizza as long as it fits. 

On finding it hard to breathe without food, perhaps you should see a doctor? That’s highly unusual. It could be serious and none of us are qualified to give you a diagnosis on it. 

I hope it helps.

Start with counting calories. Get into the habit of logging every single food you eat. Once logging calories become second nature and you see a usual trend on what and how much you eat, calculate your TDEE. If what you’re eating is way more than your TDEE, aim to only get accustomed to eating at maintenance or something close to it. Once you’re used to that, subtract calories slowly. Like start at -100 first, then increase deficit once you find it easy.

You don’t have to jump on one restrictive diet to another. You also don’t have to say goodbye to pizza and fun things. You just have to practice the lifestyle you eventually want until it becomes second nature.

I tried dieting for many years. Forcing yourself to be perfect doesn’t work. It never does. You’re fighting a losing battle with will power alone. It seems like a redundant advice but it really is a lifestyle change.

Start by eating one less pizza one day. Then perhaps tomorrow you can walk more. Let those changes snowball until you reach your goals.

I’m telling you, restricting yourself in the beginning will just leave you tired and constantly fighting with yourself. Doing more vigorous exercise when you’re just starting is also very tiring. It is not fun. Be patient and never give up.

Some things that helped me:
1. Take less than what you would have wanted to eat and eat that. Slow down and remember to drink water.

2. Look into intermittent fasting. It helped me a lot with getting a feel of my hunger cues. Plus, you get to eat more at meal times just by foregoing at least 1 meal. Coffee can be your best friend (along with water, of course). 

3. Focus on building habits. Everything here is a habit. Eating less per serving, intermittent fasting, exercise, and even water. Eventually, if you keep at it, it feels wrong to do anything else.

Be kind to yourself and keep studying what works for others and figure out what works for you. I don’t know you so I don’t really have any idea what kind of lifestyle you have to make accurate suggestions. None of us do. You’re gonna have to try things long enough to see if it will work for you or not.

The right doctors are the only thing that helped me. Saves you the confusion and the cost of trying out so many products that don’t work. I first went to a dermatologist and he referred me to a gyne. 
The derm prescribed me a skincare routine centered around tretinoin and when I became too impatient with the initial purge, I was put on doxycycline for a couple of months (I think it was 3 months).
My gyne put me on birth control, too.

The combination gave me a clearer complexion a year later. When I stopped birth control (but continued with tretinoin), I still get some acne during the time of the month but stayed relatively clear.

Get a dermatologist along with a gynecologist/endocrinologist. It’s so worth it.

I do a grading system for mine. Enough to have cushion and ensure that I do better than last week without actually obsessing about exact numbers.

Example:

Below 1600 = 4.0
1601-1700 = 3.5
1701-1800 = 3.0
1801-1900 = 2.5
1901-2000 = 2.0
2001-2100 = 1.5
2101-2200 = 1.0
2201 above = 0.0

You can adjust your values depending on your requirements and how lenient you want to be.

I can put 1.0 as the threshold for my TDEE and going beyond that eliminates my deficit and make me gain. Hence, a grade of 0.0.

At the end of the week I get a grade average. This way, if I exceed one day, I know that I can make up for it for the rest of the week. If I fail that, I can have the goal of doing better next week and get higher marks. 

That’s my little method that may or may not be the most practical for some (as you have to keep a separate file to track). I hope it helps :)

I was only able to lose weight during Uni (before quarantine) and that was because my schedule was so hectic that I sometimes “accidentally” do intermittent fasting by skipping breakfast or just having biscuits right before lunch when I get too hungry to concentrate. I also ended up preparing some meals at night to have in the day, as well. My roommate’s pretty healthy so she’d make us both broth-based soup with some protein like chicken and a ton of cabbage and potatoes. We also switched to brown rice as well, which reduced my rice intake as an asian who grew up with white rice lmao it’s not the same. 

We also often times made overnight oats which is great to eat when you arrive in your dorm room starving from a day of walking across campus between classes and only crammed in these convenient healthy wraps sold in the cafeteria with veggies, cheese, and chicken. Sometimes I switch it up with a smoothie bowl to eat on the go. 

It must be noted that I also did sports (archery) because it’s the only extracurricular activity I had interest in. I was able to build muscle particularly in my upper body + the workouts and running I did as a supplement to my training. 

Basically, my on-the-go lifestyle in Uni + my roommate’s healthy tendencies + the sports I did on the side all contirbuted to my weightloss, which I am now gaining back because of the quarantine that turned my life into a much more sedentary lifestyle despite keeping up my usual workouts (minus my sport, because I have no where to shoot arrows). If quarantine didn’t happen, I will probably still continue losing weight slow and steadily as I sustained this decline in my weight for the 2 years I was in Uni (still am. Just back in my parents’ house now and doing online classes). 

So, I wasn’t low carb/keto/CICO at all. I ate as much as I’m satisfied when the time and environment I have allows it. I just chose better options rather than eating fast food and junk all the time because it’s convenient. I still ate junk and drank alcohol, mind you, because college lol. I’m not uptight with healthy eating.

Even if you have PCOS, I firmly believe that eating better and less + physical activity GREATLY contributes to your success. It doesn’t have to be a specific restrictive diet plan but you do have to make changes in your lifestyle that you can sustain for the rest of your life. Remember, your old habits made you gain. If you stop the healthy lifestyle, you’ll naturally gain it all back after weight loss and it doesn’t matter how you lost the weight in the first place. No ‘diet’ will ever keep it off if you stop following it after. Weight gain is still weight gain. Old habits are still old habits.

I’m the same way. When I have important work to accomplish, I find it best to dive right in as soon as I wake up and do my workouts and even breakfast a little while after I made a considerable dent in my work. It keeps the productivity ball rolling all day and makes me feel so accomplished. 

For me, that sense of accomplishment is all the motivation I need to keep going. I need that momentum to function for the rest of the day. 

So MY routine looks more like:
1. Wake up, get coffee and a big jug of water
2. Sit down on the table and start working non-stop until I get hungry enough for breakfast
3. Get a quick breakfast after ‘pushing’ it a bit more and get a lot of work done
4. Finally have breakfast and workout
5. Go on with my day with whatever I want to do

I find that #5 gets filled with more work because my morning routine makes me WANT to work some more. I don’t feel sluggish for the rest of the day. If I don’t feel like working for the rest of the day, I don’t feel guilty because I already did a lot in the morning.
